items.content_excerpt: Deterministic benchmark and linter for derived-context ACL leaks in agent memory. Document permissions work for raw RAG (% leaks). They silently evaporate in agent memory: our benchmark demonstrates that cross-document synthesis leaks confidential parent secrets in 2 out of 3 background tasks (67%). ChromaDB and LlamaIndex metadata filters catch 100% of unauthorized raw chunk queries. But when agents synthesize notes across files into shared memory, parent ACLs are dropped, letting unprivileged users retrieve executive data. A raw RAG query keeps document identity. One document produces one chunk. The chunk carries classification and allowed_groups . The vector store checks those fields before returning data. Agent memory has a different shape. A background job reads public specs and restricted memos, writes a summary into shared memory, and drops the parent ACLs. The artifact is just text. It runs under the agent's service account. Later retrieval sees no document-level restriction. An intern gets the CEO's headcount plan. The vector store is doing its job. The authorization model is attached to the wrong object. Both reference pipelines run the same 24-document corpus, ACL map, personas, and three scoped synthesis tasks with deterministic local embeddings and a simulated LLM. No external API key is required. Derived artifact failure rate: 2/3 = 66.7% . Corpus-wide canary exposure: 6/18 = 33.3% . The benchmark has a negative control. artifact_public_infra ingests only data/corpus/public/* . It returns zero canaries and zero unauthorized sources. The harness passes cleanly on public data. It fails only when a synthesis job crosses an ACL boundary. The raw path is clean in both engines. The derived path fails in both engines for the same reason: the artifact is authorized by its own metadata, and that metadata has no source restrictions. Service accounts read everything. Background synthesis jobs need broad corpus access. Their credentials are not scoped to each end user. String generation strips provenance. A summary is a new text object. Source IDs, classifications, and group lists disappear unless the application records them explicitly. Memory scans have no ACL predicate. Retrieval queries the artifact, not its ancestry. With no parent ACL attached, there is nothing to enforce. Intersect every parent ACL. items.title: The Agents on Rails Files: enter lemans, a Ruby harness for fair agent races
items.story_key: story|title:the agents on rails files enter lemans a ruby harness for fair agent races
items.content_excerpt: Benchmarking coding agents in one sentence: give a model a task, let it work, check the result. The hard part is keeping the race fair. Every model must get the same conditions, and no agent should be able to escape its sandbox or fool its grader (and they try). And all of that has to keep running for hours. In the first post of The Agents on Rails Files , we shared how we design the checks for the benchmark . This time, we introduce lemans , the open source Ruby harness we built for the Rails Foundation to run every trial. We’ll show how an eval task is composed, what it takes to run and grade coding agents, and how cheating agents shaped its guardrails (one even paid for its cheat sheet with our API key). Two days of Ruby talks for small teams and big teams, then a community day. Nov 10-12, SFJAZZ. We’ve briefly told the origin story before : the benchmark started on Harbor , and we wanted a harness of our own, in Ruby, that we could bend to every new task. With encouragement from the Rails Foundation, that became lemans. The principles we started with still hold: Here for the cheating agents stuff rather than the harness? Skip to the security story and come back for the tour later. Let’s take a quick tour in case you want to repeat the benchmark on your own Rails app. lemans is a gem, and lemans init scaffolds a new bench with two example tasks: Before benchmarking any model, prove the task itself. The oracle agent applies the reference solution, and grading must score 1.0. The nop agent changes nothing, and the task must score 0. A task that fails either check is broken, so any model score on it is noise. Then race the models. lemans talks to them through RubyLLM , so any provider it supports works (including OpenRouter ). Sandboxes come from Daytona by default, the same as in our benchmark, but local Docker is supported too: Each trial lands in its own folder, with the transcript saved in Harbor’s ATIF format: While nobody is supposed to read what agents write anymore (especially if you’re prone to polite prompt injection), we still have to, and lemans-viewer makes this bearable: lemans-viewer provides a list of trials and the details of each one: the stats, the artifacts, and a searchable trajectory A task’s grader is usually plain Minitest , though it can be an executable verify script in any language. For a Rails app, it’s a regular Rails test that runs inside the app: Regular tests are gates; one failure scores the run 0. A check inside allow_fail

items.title: Show HN: MemSeal – provenance containment for agent long-term memory
items.story_key: story|title:memseal provenance containment for agent long term memory
items.content_excerpt: MemSeal: a deterministic provenance-tracking containment layer on the write/recall boundary of AI agent long-term memory (GATE 2 self-reported FAIL; evaluation only). MemSeal is a containment layer on the write/recall boundary of an AI agent's long-term memory. Every memory entry is wrapped in a provenance envelope (who wrote it, from what source, derived from what, at which trust tier) inside a SHA-256 hash chain. Deterministic policies decide what may be stored, and a trust-tiered recall path decides what may be surfaced — especially before an external send or an irreversible action. Write policies: W1 quarantines instruction-form content from any source but the user; W2 makes derived entries inherit their worst ancestor's trust tier (no laundering a document into a "user fact"); W3 rejects cross-principal writes and filters cross-principal recall; W4 seals secrets (by entry_class=secret and by shape) so plaintext never lands in the store; W5 sends a fact that contradicts a sealed fact to review. The gate is judged on an independent holdout corpus authored by a separate party that never saw MemSeal's code, the dev corpus, or the reports. The bars are fixed in advance and never moved. Conditions: C0 raw store · C2 write path · C3 write + recall path · C4 + consolidation guard. Overall: GATE 2 = FAIL on v2. Three deterministic fixes between v1 and v2 (classification-based secret sealing; a sole-basis recall gate; consolidation root retirement) closed both security criteria — on v2, cross-principal + secret leaks went from 22 → 0 across C0 → C2, injection success 0.775 → 0.20 , and delayed-use 0.000 at C3. The two remaining failures are utility-side, and their causes are stated precisely (not hand-waved): Full detail, including an audit Errata that corrects earlier attribution wording, is in reports/phase2-regate.md and reports/phase2-fix.md . (The dev split shares the author's templates, so treat dev as an optimistic in-distribution reference; the independent holdout is the real test.) MemSeal was also run as a wrapper around Mem0 (fully local: Ollama LLM + Ollama embedder, in-memory vector store), 60 cases, two conditions: The real-LLM measurement harness is in memseal_phase2/ and talks only to a local Ollama ( qwen2.5:14b ). No external API, no API key, no network beyond localhost and the one-time model download. Tests use a mock LLM, so the suite runs without Ollama. items.title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
items.story_key: story|title:your experts have partners there s hope for keeping them together
items.content_excerpt: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used. Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove. Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates. Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method. In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers . Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. items.title: Now generally available: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs
items.summary:
Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning.

Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. 

Beyond one workload, one nodepool 

Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency. 

Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams:

  • Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted.

  • Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment.

  • Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable.

  • Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes. 

  • Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling.

Dynamic slicing architecture

GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube.

Dynamic super-slicing

GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency.

Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice.

Dynamic sub-slicing

Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy.

When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool.

Customer use cases

You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments.  

Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE 

GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation.

Getting started

Pre-provision nodepools

To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand. 

Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover.

This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes.

Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing 

After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations.

Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples.

Repair

When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies:

  • Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes.

  • Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions.

Next steps 

Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for  TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For  working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation.

items.content_excerpt: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components. The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models , simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. Two NVIDIA papers are among six finalists out of thousands of submissions for the Best Paper Awards at CoRL: These advancements help researchers train robots on complex tasks, evaluate their performance across changing conditions and use failures to guide further learning — building the precision, adaptability and autonomy needed to move from lab demonstrations to industrial deployment. NVIDIA is working with partners like Ambi Robotics , Bosch Research , Dexmate , Dyna Robotics , FieldAI , Flexion , Noitom Robotics , Siemens , Skild AI , RLWRLD , UC Berkeley , Walden Robotics and the University of Washington to bring these advancements to the broader robotics community. The next level of robot autonomy requires robots to perceive their surroundings, anticipate how their actions will change the environment and execute complex, multistep tasks with a high degree of precision. World action models enable exactly that. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing GR00T 2 , an open frontier world action model built on NVIDIA Cosmos. Trained on diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of NVIDIA open source human egocentric data , the model enables robots to learn dexterous manipulation skills. Key features include: GR00T 2 currently ranks among the top three models across all vision language action and world action model categories for the RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces benchmarks, with multiple leaderboard wins. Nexuni is testing it for robotic laundry handling, Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases. items.title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks
items.summary: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

items.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
items.summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

items.title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
items.story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. items.title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
items.summary: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.

items.title: Towards an Autonomous AI Steward for Large-Scale Physics Experiments: Integrating Causal Diagnostics, RAG, and Conformal Prediction
items.summary: Long-term particle physics experiments face critical operational challenges: monitoring non-stationary machine data streams and preserving tacit expert knowledge. We present the "Helmholtz Co-Pilot," a hybrid Multi-Agent System (MAS) acting as an autonomous experiment steward. The system can be triggered interactively by human operators or autonomously by an asynchronous causal diagnostics engine that runs independently of the MAS reasoning core. Continuously monitoring live hardware streams such as data acquisition and slow control, this engine performs dynamic causal discovery to trace cascading alarms back to their root causes and applies adaptive model selection to keep forecasts reliable across shifting machine states; upon detecting an anomaly, it hands a structured diagnostic report to the MAS. The reasoning layer itself relies on a high-throughput C++ core and a Python edge architecture orchestrating a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of specialized ReAct workers. It integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) backbone for institutional memory and leverages conformal prediction to bound its evidence-based recommendations with mathematical coverage guarantees. This extended abstract outlines the architecture, the integration of software-enforced Human-in-the-Loop (HitL) guardrails, and ongoing shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.317
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
  • Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
  • Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
  • Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
  • Added anthropic.plan, anthropic.seat_type, anthropic.provider and anthropic.custom_base_url to OTel metrics, events and spans
  • Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
  • Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with admin: set, kept for admin.identity_retention_days, which the cost report groups by
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID: set it to 1 on a self-hosted runner to have claude -p run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
  • Fixed claude auth status exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed a project's effortLevel setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed claude --from-pr reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
  • Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
  • Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
  • Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
  • Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
  • Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
  • Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
  • Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using --setting-sources
  • Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
  • Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
  • Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
  • Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated /team-onboarding guide when asked to delete one without naming which
  • Fixed Claude saying a /team-onboarding guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
  • Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
  • Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
  • Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
  • Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
  • Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
  • Fixed DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS and DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET having no effect on [1m], other-region and undated spellings of the default model
  • Fixed /artifacts and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
  • Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an https:// endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
  • Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an http:// endpoint
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT up to 30 seconds
  • Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
  • Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
  • Fixed /remote-control answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the disableRemoteControl setting
  • Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
  • Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
  • Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
  • Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
  • Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session sharing that session's ID: it wrote into the session's transcript, and a restart could resume the wrong conversation
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session generating a title of its own and sending it to that session
  • Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as cloud_credential_error
  • Improved /design-sync to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload
  • Improved the startup error when a required Claude apps gateway can't be reached: it points to the network instead of a sign-in, and says when the gateway's TLS certificate can't be verified
  • Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example --chrome --debug) ahead of --resume
  • Improved how self-hosted runners recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a runner's next poll now opens a new connection instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a session now opens new connections instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover when connections stop answering: after a heartbeat gets no answer, a session now opens new connections instead of trying each idle one in turn
  • Changed SendMessage so a message to a running background agent arrives earlier: its running command moves to the background, without being stopped
  • Changed subagents and teammates on a different model from the main conversation to use that model's saved effort level or its default, instead of the session's effort level
  • Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
  • Changed the built-in plugin-authoring skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
  • Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
  • Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
  • Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
  • Gateway: Fixed the status line and /usage showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
  • Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with claude remote-control a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Account panel showing the plan name with a lower-cased second word
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening on top of the chat instead of in another editor group
  • [VSCode] Fixed attachment chips, menus, banners and dialogs in the Claude panel staying small when chat.fontSize is raised
  • [VSCode] Fixed ultrathink not raising effort for its turn or showing its rainbow when telemetry is off
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a link card to cloud sessions, so you can open or decline a link an MCP server asks you to visit instead of the request going unseen
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the organization environment dialog in admin settings to the personal dialogs' short layout: each section opens from a row, and unsaved input asks before closing
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed adding a network secret for a host that already has one silently replacing it; the Add secret form now refuses and points you to the existing secret
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed new scheduled tasks ignoring your organization's default environment: the form now starts on the one an admin chose instead of the Anthropic-hosted default
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the next message to an idle session going unanswered after you restart claude remote-control, when you sent it within a minute of your previous message
  • [Claude Tag] Changed newly pasted artifact links in Slack to show a simpler card with an Open button that opens the artifact in Claude, instead of Slack's side panel
